state.case_summary:
A 60-year-old Saudi man presented with an 18-month history of erythroderma affecting his entire body and face. Five years earlier, he had developed slightly pruritic, slowly progressive erythematous lesions on his trunk and retroauricular area that were misdiagnosed as severe eczema and treated with multiple courses of oral prednisolone and cyclosporine without improvement. On examination, there were confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques with overlying thick greasy scales on the face, neck, trunk, genitalia, upper and lower extremities, palms, and soles, with sparing of the nails and scalp. Bilateral lower‐lid ectropion was present; there was no palpable lymphadenopathy. Three skin punch biopsies (lower back, left buttock, right upper extremity) demonstrated epidermotropism of a large number of atypical lymphocytes—single and in clusters—and a superficial dermal band‐like lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal fibrosis. Direct immunofluorescence was negative for fibrinogen, C3, IgA, IgM, and IgG. Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells positive for CD3 and CD45RO but negative for CD4, CD8, and CD7; CD30 was positive in fewer than 25% of lymphocytes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Mycosis fungoides
B. Sézary syndrome
C. Cutaneous γ/δ T
D. Extranodal NK/T
E. Primary cutaneous peripheral T
F. None
G. None
H. None
